metadata.title: Christa Pike says there is ‘pain in my mind and in my soul’ one month after failed execution

sources.news_title: Christa Pike describes constant pain in first statement since her failed execution - WSVN 7News | Miami News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
(AP) — Christa Pike said Friday she remains in constant pain, struggles to speak and has been largely isolated in a prison hospital after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month.
In her first public statement since, Pike said she’s “deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”
“I continue to think about my victim’s family,” she said, “and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.”
Pike and her boyfriend tortured and stabbed a 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, to death in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time, making her one of the youngest women sentenced to death. Slemmer’s mother traveled from Florida to witness Pike’s execution.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably didn’t enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered. Unconscious, she was hospitalized on a ventilator for days, and at one point her lawyers said they didn’t expect her to survive.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” Pike said. “And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Pike said she had been prepared to die in peace, but instead woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed. She said she’s “searching for meaning in what happened to me.”
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” Pike said in a statement dictated to her legal team from prison.
Pike remains sentenced to die, and her attorneys want Republican Gov. Bill Lee to change that to life in prison. However, Lee told reporters this week, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
The governor has tapped a former U.S. attorney to conduct an independent review of the failed execution, and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled for this year.
Pike’s attorneys, meanwhile, asked a federal judge Friday to allow her to interact with other prisoners instead of being isolated in the infirmary. They said her isolation violates a 2024 agreement that ended her mostly solitary confinement and allowed her to work, eat, exercise and have social contact with other women.
“Her renewed isolation has caused, and will continue to cause, significant psychological harm and trauma,” Pike’s legal team wrote.
Pike’s lethal injection was plagued by problems. Her attorneys had warned that her small veins and diagnosis of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting disorder, could make IV access difficult.
In a court document, her attorney Randy Spivey said the execution team struggled to get working IV lines in Pike’s arms and expressed concern that a vein might be “blowing.” Pike remained awake for much of the lethal injection, saying her arm hurt and burned before falling unconscious. The execution began just before 7:30 p.m. and an ambulance arrived at the prison about an hour and 45 minutes later.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.
In a 2025 deposition released with court documents this week, prison Warden Kenneth Nelson said the execution team doesn’t practice inserting IV lines during training sessions, at the directive of the prison commissioner. Nelson said he did not know why the practice was discontinued or when the order was given.
Practicing insertion of IVs was part of Tennessee’s prior execution protocol, but it is not included in the state’s new protocol.
Dorinda Carter, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction, said she could not comment on the filing because of pending litigation.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike’s failed execution. The governor named Christopher Hansen as interim commissioner.

US execution survivor is isolated 'in constant pain'
US death row inmate Christa Pike, in her first statement after she survived a botched execution a month ago, says she is in constant physical and mental pain and largely isolated from other people in a prison hospital ward.
Pike is being held in the Debra K Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the Tennessee prison where she has been housed for over 30 years after her conviction for a 1995 murder.
In a statement released on Friday by her lawyers, to whom she dictated it, she said she continued to think about her victim's family and the "terrible pain and loss they have endured".
She said her isolation was causing mental pain by reminding her of the 28 years she spent in solitary confinement.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul," Pike said.
Pike, 50, was taken from the execution chamber at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections failed to kill her on September 30.
She was released from the hospital and sent to the Johnson centre on October 10, days after her lawyers said she had regained consciousness and was speaking.
In her statement, she thanked the first responders, doctors and nurses who cared for her after the attempted execution.
Pike said she did not know why she survived the execution, nor what would happen to her next.
She said the love and support she has received from people around the world has given her strength.
"To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words," Pike said.
A Tennessee judge has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to their failed attempt to execute her, a development one of her lawyers called the "first of many steps to preserve and enforce her constitutional rights".
Her lawyers have called the botched attempt a violation of the Constitution's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of 2026 while investigators look into the botched execution of Pike and a similar failure in May involving another inmate.
Lee, who denied Pike's clemency appeal to commute her sentence to life in prison two days before the execution attempt, told reporters earlier this week that he expected her sentence would remain unchanged "unless determined otherwise by the courts".
She would have been the first woman Tennessee put to death since the early 19th century.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and a third companion lured Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate in Knoxville, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
Pike and Shipp were convicted of first-degree murder. Shipp, whose age at the time made him ineligible for the death penalty, received a life sentence and remains in prison.
The third person involved testified against Pike and Shipp as part of a plea deal and received probation.

Christa Pike’s lawyers have filed an emergency motion in federal court, arguing that Tennessee prison officials are violating a previous agreement about her conditions in prison.
In 2022, Pike sued the Tennessee Department of Correction after spending decades in solitary confinement.
A settlement reached in September 2024 allowed her to work, eat meals, exercise and socialise with other women in custody.

They want the previous agreement to be followed through, which would allow her to interact with other prisoners again, as far as her medical condition and safety permit.
“The motion was filed on an emergency basis because each day of continued isolation causes further harm to Ms. Pike,” her lawyers said.
“It asks the court to order the State to end her isolation and restore the protections in the agreement as far as her medical needs and safety allow. Counsel continues to hope for a cooperative resolution that serves Ms. Pike’s health and well-being.”
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during an attempted execution last month (30 September).
The 50-year-old was discharged from hospital and is now back at the Debra K Johnson Rehabilitation Centre, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years.
Pike has also released a personal statement detailing her ongoing pain and recovery.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul," she said.

Christa Pike's statement in full
"One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men's prison prepared to die.
"I had made my peace. I had told the people who loved me, supported me and stood by me through the years I was grateful for them. I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness.
"Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain. There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger. But healing is not the same as being okay.
"Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison's medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me. That isolation brings its own kind of pain. I spent 28 years in solitary confinement and much of what I am experiencing today is a repeat of that condition.
"I am searching for meaning in what happened to me. One thing that has given me strength is the extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. I am overwhelmed by the kindness and prayers of people I have known for years and complete strangers who have never met me.
"To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words. It is humbling, and it has touched me more deeply than I can explain.

I also want to thank my attorneys and everyone who has fought for me, stood beside me and refused to give up on me.

sources.text:
When Christa Pike finally entered the lethal injection room after spending 30 agonizing years on Tennessee’s death row, she was at peace, ready to face her impending execution. When she awoke in a hospital following the states’ botched execution attempt, she says she was disoriented and in excruciating pain, all thanks to the barbarity of lethal injection.
According to the Associated Press, Pike has been in constant pain in the month following Tennessee’s horrifically botched execution attempts. On September 30, state executioners made two attempts to administer pentobarbital, a highly controversial barbiturate the sale of which to US penal institutions is restricted by international bodies like the European Union.
Observers at the time noted at least seven needles piercing Pike’s arm during one injection, followed by a 90-minute period where the woman appeared to be snapping in and out of consciousness. After it became apparent that the second injection failed, Pike was rushed to the hospital, where she was listed in critical condition.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said in her first statement since her failed execution. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Tennessee’s failure to carry out an execution 30 years in the making has become a major legal and ethical dilemma around the efficacy of lethal injection in particular, and capital punishment as a whole.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, an estimated three percent of all executions between 1890 and 2010 were botched, resulting in some 276 gruesome deaths at the hands of state authorities. Lethal injection is by far the most likely to go wrong, with an overall failure rate of over seven percent.
That being the case, Pike is one of 75 people to experience a botched lethal injection in the US, and according to the AP, the only one to ever survive the particular drug cocktail that was pumped into her arm.
“I don’t know why I survived that night,” Pike continued in her statement. “I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone.”

‘My body hurts’: Christa Pike describes pain and isolation after botched execution
Pike’s legal team has asked Republican Gov. Bill Lee to consider granting her clemency, allowing her to spend the remainder of her life in prison.
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — In her first comments since Tennessee botched her execution last month, Christa Pike said that she was in constant pain and that she had been kept largely in isolation.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” she said, according to a statement released Friday. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak.”
Pike, 50, received the death penalty for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate in Knoxville, Tenn. Pike, then 18, was one of three students who lured Slemmer into the woods, slashed at her with a box cutter, and beat her.
In the statement, which she dictated to her legal team, Pike said she had been prepared to die the morning of Sept. 30. She had said her goodbyes to her loved ones and supporters. She told the people in the death chamber she was leaving them “in loving kindness.”
But then she woke up alone, confused and in pain, according to the statement. She was the first person to survive after receiving a lethal dose of the drug pentobarbital.
“I had not contemplated life beyond that night,” Pike said, “and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”
She added, “I am searching for meaning in what happened to me.”
The mother of Slemmer, May Martinez, was in favor of the execution and has rejected Pike’s expressions of remorse in the years since the crime. Pike said she was thinking about Slemmer’s family and “the terrible pain and loss they have endured.”
The execution, initially delayed in a flurry of last-minute legal maneuvering, went ahead the evening of Sept. 30. In court documents this month, Randy Spivey, one of Pike’s lawyers who witnessed the execution, described nearly an hour in which members of the team responsible for placing the IV struggled to do so.
At one point, Spivey said, one team member said that a vein “might be blowing,” acknowledging that a vein might have been damaged in the process. In excerpts from a 2025 deposition released in court this week, Kenneth Nelson, the warden at the prison where executions take place, said the team contracted for the execution did not practice what to do if they had a hard time inserting an IV.
It took about 30 minutes to verify the authenticity of the first 911 call for an ambulance from the prison. Pike was in a private Nashville hospital for more than a week, where staff “treated me with compassion, dignity, and respect,” she said.
The botched handling of the execution has drawn scrutiny as the state’s second failed attempt at capital punishment this year. After Pike’s execution attempt, Frank Strada, the embattled head of the Tennessee Department of Correction, said he would step down.
Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican who is term-limited, paused all executions for the remainder of his term and ordered an independent investigation into the practice. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor, has said she believes Pike should face execution a second time, calling for the use of the electric chair instead of lethal injection.
Pike’s legal team has asked Lee to consider granting her clemency, allowing her to spend the remainder of her life in prison. On Wednesday, Lee told reporters, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
Pike spent most of her three decades in prison in isolation, until a 2024 settlement allowed her some physical interaction with other women in the prison. In her statement Friday, she said being alone in the infirmary was a painful repeat of that treatment, even as her recovery continued.
“I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger,” she said. Her long-term prognosis, her legal team said, remains unclear.
“I don’t know why I survived that night — I don’t know what comes next,” Pike said. She added, “For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”

One month after Tennessee tried and failed to execute Christa Pike, the convicted killer is speaking publicly about what happened inside the death chamber.
Her message is blunt: she says she remains in constant pain, struggles to speak and blames state officials for what she called their “incompetence.”

That sets up a legal and moral showdown with two very different questions at its center: What accountability does the state face for a lethal-injection attempt that went catastrophically wrong — and does that failure alter the death sentence Pike received for the brutal murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer?
Those questions should not be blurred together.
According to the Associated Press, Pike dictated her first public statement since the September 30 execution attempt to her attorneys from a prison infirmary. The account describes her as conscious but still struggling to speak, living with persistent pain and isolated from the rest of death row while lawyers pursue medical records, an independent explanation of the failed procedure and a commutation request that would replace execution with life imprisonment.
“I was prepared to die,” Pike said in the statement.
She said she later woke up in a hospital confused, frightened and in severe pain. Pike now says she is living with constant physical and mental suffering, has trouble speaking and remains isolated while recovering in the prison medical unit.
“I was not prepared for their incompetence,” she said.
The AP account says Pike remains in the prison infirmary, separated from the rest of death row while she recovers. Her lawyers say even speaking is difficult and that she has to stop frequently because of pain.
Her statement also acknowledges Slemmer’s relatives, saying she cannot imagine the pain the family continues to carry. That acknowledgment arrives as Pike’s legal team presses Lee to commute her sentence and argues that forcing her through another execution would amount to unconstitutional punishment.

— KTVU (@KTVU) October 30, 2026
Tennessee administered two doses of the sedative pentobarbital during the execution attempt, but Pike remained alive.
Her attorneys say she was rushed to a hospital unconscious, placed on a ventilator and treated for injuries that included burns and blistering on her arms. They have argued that the intravenous lines may have failed, allowing the drug to enter surrounding tissue instead of her bloodstream.
The state has not publicly accepted that explanation.
In its official September 30 media advisory, the Tennessee Department of Correction said its execution protocol had been followed and that Pike was transported to an off-site medical facility after the execution was stopped.
Medical and legal experts have focused on possible IV infiltration as one explanation for what happened, but a full outside review is still underway.
The distinction matters. There is a difference between allegations made by Pike’s legal team, the narrow account released by the state and findings that have actually been established by an independent investigation.
The advisory also identified the officials who observed the procedure, noted that media witnesses had been dismissed and said the department would provide additional information as appropriate. It did not explain why Pike survived two doses or resolve the competing medical account offered by her attorneys.

Pike also said she thinks about Slemmer’s family.

— Daily Mail US (@Daily_MailUS) October 29, 2026

It should intensify scrutiny.
The government does not get a free pass when an execution goes wrong. A state that claims the power to take a life under law must be held to the highest standard of competence, transparency and accountability.
At the same time, a botched procedure does not rewrite the murder, erase the jury’s verdict or remove Colleen Slemmer from the story.
That is the hard line Tennessee now has to walk.
The independent review must determine exactly what failed, who knew what, whether the state’s protocol was adequate and whether officials’ public account matches the medical evidence.
The courts will then have to decide whether another execution attempt would violate Pike’s constitutional rights. Gov. Lee will have to decide whether clemency is warranted.
But those decisions should be made on verified evidence — not slogans, political pressure or an attempt by either side to pretend only one victim exists in this painful case.
Pike is alive and describing serious suffering. Slemmer was murdered and can no longer speak for herself.
Tennessee owes the public the full truth about both.

The 50-year-old death row inmate says she remains in physical and emotional distress after surviving two lethal injections, as Tennessee investigates the failed execution and her attorneys challenge any attempt to carry out her death sentence again.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived a failed lethal injection Sept. 30, released her first public statement Friday, describing persistent physical pain, difficulty speaking and emotional distress one month after prison officials attempted to execute her for the 1995 murder of a teenage classmate.
Pike, 50, dictated the statement to her attorneys while recovering at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville. She said she entered the execution chamber expecting to die and awoke several days later in a hospital, confused and suffering from injuries sustained during the procedure.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” Pike said in the statement released Oct. 30. “And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
According to ABC News’ report on her first public remarks, Pike criticized the handling of her execution and expressed concern about the suffering experienced by those involved, including the family of her murder victim, Colleen Slemmer.
“I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said. “I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.”
Pike had been scheduled to die by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Prison officials administered two doses of pentobarbital, but the procedure failed to cause her death.
Attorneys who witnessed the execution reported significant problems establishing intravenous access, including repeated attempts to insert needles into her arms. The procedure continued for nearly two hours before officials stopped the execution and transferred Pike for emergency medical treatment.
Pike subsequently spent approximately five days in a coma while receiving intensive medical care. Her attorneys reported that her arms were swollen and blistered following the unsuccessful injections.
In her statement published by Sky News, Pike recalled the hours leading up to the execution, saying she had prepared herself emotionally and said goodbye to friends and supporters.
“One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men’s prison prepared to die,” she said. “I had made my peace. I had told the people who loved me, supported me and stood by me through the years I was grateful for them. I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness.”
“Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain,” Pike continued.
She acknowledged that her physical condition has gradually improved but said the experience continues to affect her.
“I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger. But healing is not the same as being okay.”
Pike’s failed execution has prompted renewed scrutiny of Tennessee’s lethal injection procedures and the state’s ability to carry out executions without causing prolonged suffering.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is believed to be the only person in the United States known to have survived an execution attempt after lethal injection drugs were administered.
The incident followed another unsuccessful Tennessee execution attempt earlier this year involving death row inmate Tony Carruthers. In that case, prison personnel were unable to establish intravenous access despite spending more than an hour attempting to do so. Gov. Bill Lee subsequently granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve.
Following Pike’s execution, Lee ordered an independent investigation and suspended further Tennessee executions through the end of 2026. The governor has not agreed to commute Pike’s death sentence.
The investigation will examine the state’s lethal injection procedures, the conduct of execution personnel and the circumstances that allowed Pike to survive despite receiving the drugs intended to cause her death.

“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” she said. “Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”

She said she woke up confused in her hospital bed several days after the execution attempt.

It’s the first public comment attributed to Pike since the botched execution. She is the only person to ever survive being injected with lethal chemicals in an execution, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
The failure to execute Pike upset Slemmer’s family, who previously said the attention on Pike’s condition has taken attention away from the victim.
“I think the state owes me a big apology,” May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, told CNN affiliate WTLV a few weeks ago. Pike was returned to prison earlier this month after a 10-day hospitalization and has continued receiving medical care, according to her lawyers.
“Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison’s medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me,” Pike said in Friday’s statement. “That isolation brings its own kind of pain. I spent 28 years in solitary confinement and much of what I am experiencing today is a repeat of that condition.”
Pike’s attorneys filed an emergency motion on Friday requesting she be removed from “indefinite isolation in the prison infirmary,” where she’s been “cut off from all other inmates” since she was discharged from the hospital earlier this month.
The attorneys said the state of Tennessee is violating the 2024 settlement agreement allowing Pike to work, eat, socialize and exercise alongside other women in the general population at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center.
“State officials have kept her alone in the prison infirmary, cut off from all other women in custody and with no expected end date for her isolation,” Angie Bergman, Brian Roark and Hannah Webber, Pike’s lawyers, said in a statement. “Despite repeated warnings that this conduct not only harms Ms. Pike but is in direct violation of the clear terms of the Settlement Agreement, the State has failed to make any accommodations or engage in any attempt at a meaningful resolution.”
The emergency motion asked for the settlement agreement to be enforced and for an end to “her indefinite isolation” and for accommodation for “group meals, recreation, work and other social interaction,” according to the federal court filing.
“The motion was filed on an emergency basis because each day of continued isolation causes further harm to Ms. Pike,” the attorneys said in the statement.
The Tennessee Department of Correction doesn’t comment on pending litigation as agency policy, a spokesperson said.
The state Attorney General’s Office didn’t immediately respond to CNN’s email request for comment.
Pike is fighting what will likely be a protracted legal battle to prevent a second attempt to put her to death. Her attorneys filed a complaint in January seeking to delay her execution because of the state’s new lethal injection protocol, saying it was untested and “sure or very likely to result in unnecessary and superadded pain and suffering, terror, and disgrace.”
“The new protocol does not provide for any life saving measures, in violation of the Plaintiffs rights under the United States Constitution and the Tennessee Constitution in the event that the execution fails,” Pike’s legal team warned at the time.
Pike’s legal team has asked a judge to amend their complaint to reflect what happened to her on September 30. On Thursday, the court ruled Pike has until late January to make a new filing, giving her extra time due to her current medical condition.
State is investigating what went wrong
In the immediate aftermath of the botched execution, Tennessee’s Republican Gov. Bill Lee ordered an investigation into what went wrong in the death chamber and indefinitely postponed another execution scheduled this year.
Earlier this month, Lee announced state Correction Commissioner Frank Strada would step down following the backlash after the attempted execution.
On Friday, the governor’s office said Christopher Hansen would serve as the interim commissioner of the state Department of Correction effective immediately, while also keeping his current duties as assistant commissioner of community supervision.
“Chris Hansen is a committed public servant with decades of experience in corrections and public safety,” Lee said in a statement. “His knowledge of the Tennessee Department of Correction makes him uniquely qualified to lead, and I am grateful for his willingness to serve Tennesseans during this transition.”
Lee is not inclined to commute Pike’s sentence and take the death penalty off the table, he told reporters this week in Nashville.
“She’s still incarcerated under the laws of the State of Tennessee,” Lee said, according to CNN affiliate WSMV. “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Eduardo Cuevas and Avni Trivedi contributed to this report.

Christa Pike survived an execution by lethal injection in the US.
Christa Pike has released her first statement since surviving her execution in September. The convicted murderer was meant to die by lethal execution on September 30. However, after being given two doses of lethal drug pentobarbital, she remained alive, and was taken to hospital. A few days later, she woke up in a hospital bed "confused and in pain", she said in a newly released statement today.
In a statement dictated to her legal team, Pike said she had made peace with the fact she would be executed and die a month ago. She said: "One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men's prison prepared to die.
"I had made my peace. I had told the people who loved me, supported me and stood by me through the years I was grateful for them. I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness."
However, the inmate said, she woke up days after she was meant to have died in a hospital room. Describing the first moments she regained consciousness after the botched execution attempt, she said: "Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain."
She went on to describe her current health conditions, saying: "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

The inmate then described her current living conditions, saying that after spending 28 years in solitary confinement she has been "largely isolated in the prison's medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me".
She added: "I am searching for meaning in what happened to me. One thing that has given me strength is the extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. I am overwhelmed by the kindness and prayers of people I have known for years and complete strangers who have never met me.
"To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words. It is humbling, and it has touched me more deeply than I can explain.
"I also want to thank the first responders, doctors, nurses and everyone at the hospital who cared for me. They treated me with compassion, dignity and respect. I will never forget their kindness. I also want to thank my attorneys and everyone who has fought for me, stood beside me and refused to give up on me.
"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone."
Pike was found guilty at age 18, together with her boyfriend, of beating, torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training facility in Knoxville. The case attracted widespread media attention as Colleen was discovered with an inverted pentagram - a symbol linked to satanic groups - carved into her chest.

‘I am recovering’ | Christa Pike releases statement after botched Tennessee execution
Christa Pike was convicted of a grisly Knoxville murder and sentenced to death. The State of Tennessee failed to execute her in September.
What This Story Is About
- Christa Pike, who the State of Tennessee failed to execute in September, has released her first statement since her botched execution.
Why It Matters
- It marks the first time we’ve heard directly from Pike, whose attorneys are still fighting to get her taken off death row.
What Happens Next
- Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has said he expects Pike’s sentence to stay unchanged, even after the failed September attempt.
For Context
- Following the failed execution, Tennessee’s corrections chief resigned from his role. Lawmakers have called on Lee to clean house even further at the state’s correction department.
Catch Up
- Pike is the convicted offender in the “Jobs Corps Murder,” a grisly case out of Knoxville that the then-chief of police described as “gruesome.”
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT) - Convicted murderer Christa Pike has released a statement after her botched Tennessee execution, according to her legal team.
The statement comes one month after the state failed to execute Pike via lethal injection in what has now become one of the state’s most notorious failed death sentences. In the statement, Pike speaks about her mental state leading up to the execution attempt.
“One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men’s prison prepared to die,” Pike’s statement, dictated by her legal team and shared via email, says. “I had made my peace. I had told the people who loved me, supported me and stood by me through the years I was grateful for them. I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness.”
That night, Tennessee Department of Correction staff gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital. Pike was taken to a nearby hospital after the hours-long execution attempt, where she remained for some time before being released back to the department of correction.
“Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain,” Pike says. “I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”
Pike’s statement also includes details about her condition. The death row inmate says she’s been in pain since the attempted execution.
“My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts,” she says. “I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Pike’s own physical condition isn’t the only pain she references in the statement. She also says she’s thinking of the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer, who she was convicted of torturing and killing in 1995.
“I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike says.
The failed execution attempt has split opinions not only about the state’s process when putting inmates to death, but Pike herself. In the statement, Pike references those who have argued and protested in support of her and against the state’s death penalty.
“One thing that has given me strength is the extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world,” Pike says. “I am overwhelmed by the kindness and prayers of people I have known for years and complete strangers who have never met me. To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words.”
The doctors and hospital staff who cared for Pike following the failed execution also got a reference in her statement.
“I also want to thank the first responders, doctors, nurses and everyone at the hospital who cared for me,” Pike says. “They treated me with compassion, dignity and respect. I will never forget their kindness.”
Pike was convicted in 1996 in the “Jobs Corps Murder,” a name that came about because both Pike and the victim — 19-year-old Slemmer — were members of the Jobs Corps at the time of the girl’s 1995 killing. Prosecutors and testimony have said Pike conspired with two others, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, to kill Slemmer over relationship issues. It was discovered throughout the case that the offenders had carved a pentacle into Slemmer’s chest and taken a piece of her skull as a souvenir of the grisly murder.
Pike’s execution faced complications from the beginning. Less than an hour before she was to be put to death, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals placed a stay on her execution, saying the court would hear out an appeal concerning the details of her sentencing.
Hours later, the U.S. Supreme Court lifted the stay, opening the way for Tennessee’s attempted execution.

sources.text:
'There is pain in my mind and soul': Female death row inmate Christa Pike breaks silence after botched lethal injection
Sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, she awoke three weeks ago "angry and confused" in a hospital after surviving Tennessee's botched effort to execute her.
Female death row inmate Christa Pike has said there is "pain in my mind and soul" after she survived two doses of the lethal injection.
Listen to this article
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Christa Pike, 50, said in her first public statement.
“My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, she awoke three weeks ago "angry and confused" in a hospital with a long recuperation ahead after surviving Tennessee's botched effort to execute her.
The all-female execution team requested by Pike used at least seven needles during a grueling ordeal that lasted more than two hours, and one needle was bent 90 degrees when it was pulled out, her lawyers said.
She was taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections of the caustic barbiturate pentobarbital failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.
Read More: Released 911 calls reveal confusion after Christa Pike's botched execution attempt
Her lawyers believed Pike was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day following the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, which has renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US.
Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched executions of Pike and of Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines.
Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, facing a long road to recovery, her lawyers said. She cannot swallow or eat, has pneumonia, cannot move her "tremendously swollen" hands or arms, and it is unclear if she will regain her lost mobility, they said.
Pike was sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the 1995 torture and murder of her 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer.
She is the first person known to have survived a "completed execution attempt" in the US, her lawyers say, calling it a violation of the Constitution's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments.
Pike's lawyers are unexpectedly continuing their litigation against state officials, seeking to pierce the secrecy that normally surrounds execution procedures in Tennessee and other states.
A judge in Davidson County Chancery Court, I'Ashea Myles, agreed to order Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from the failed execution, including syringes, drug packaging and lot numbers, catheters, intravenous lines and gurney restraints.
This is a breaking story. More to follow...

sources.news_title: 'I woke up confused and in pain': Christa Pike describes moments after botched execution
Christa Pike says there is ‘pain in my mind and in my soul’ one month after her failed execution
sources.text:
One month ago, Christa Pike survived what seemed impossible: a lethal injection in which two rounds of the drug had already entered her body. Medics took her from the Tennessee death chamber and she was placed on a hospital ventilator; she regained consciousness days later.
Now, Pike, the sole woman on Tennessee’s death row, says she is healing in a prison medical ward, but that the pain she still feels extends far beyond the physical.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike, 50, said in her first public statement, which her legal team shared Friday. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Pike, who has been on death row for three decades for murdering Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate, was discharged from the hospital and returned to her Nashville prison 10 days after the attempt to execute her Sept. 30 went awry. Her arms were left swollen and bruised after the execution team tried to insert intravenous lines to deliver two rounds of the lethal drug pentobarbital into her bloodstream, her legal team said. Medical experts have suggested Pike’s injuries could have been the result of incorrect needle insertion or the chemical leaking into her tissue.
Before she lost consciousness, she complained that her arm felt as if it was going to burst and that “it burns,” her lawyers said.
“I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger,” Pike said in her statement. “But healing is not the same as being okay.”

Her lawyers said Pike dictated her statement, and told NBC News that she has difficulty holding a pen and speaks in a raspy voice after having been intubated.
“She is still suffering emotionally, mentally,” one of her lawyers, Stephen Ferrell said. “That was a very traumatic event, and I don’t know that has improved or progressed.”
On the day her execution was scheduled, Pike said, she walked into the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution at peace and prepared to die after her final days were spent saying her goodbyes to her loved ones. At the execution chamber, she told witnesses that she was leaving them in “loving kindness,” in reference to a Buddhist prayer her spiritual adviser had her recite.
“I had not contemplated life beyond that night,” Pike added, “and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”
A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction on Friday declined to comment about Pike’s case, and the office of Gov. Bill Lee could not immediately be reached for comment.
In the wake of the failed execution, a department spokesperson said that it had “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office” and that “the lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective.”
Lee has ordered an independent review to “determine exactly what occurred” and said he was pausing all executions through the end of the year. He also announced Correction Commissioner Frank Strada was stepping down at the end of October. Strada said it was “in the best interests” of the state.
But whether the state might try to execute Pike again remains unknown, and it underscores an ethical paradox of the death penalty: that one must be considered sufficiently healthy before the person can be put to death.
On Wednesday, Lee did not dismiss the possibility of a second execution attempt: “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before,” he told reporters, “unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
Lee, who leaves office in January, has declined to commute Pike’s death sentence to life in prison. The Republican running to replace him next month, Sen. Marsha Blackburn, said that she would resume executions if she is elected and that she favors expanding the available methods. Her Democratic opponent, Jerri Green, has said she would block any execution while she was in office.
Pike’s lawyers said they expect a “long legal battle” if Tennessee does move forward. A judge this month sided with her defense team when it argued that the state must preserve evidence related to the attempted execution, including syringes, IV lines, drugs and personnel logs.
At the time, state prosecutors said that there was “no pending execution order” and that they had not heard of one coming.
The mother of Pike’s victim, May Martinez, has said Tennessee needs to “make this right” and not remove Pike from death row. Martinez could not immediately be reached for comment.
In 1995, Pike and two other people worked together to torture, slash and bludgeon to death Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps program in Knoxville. Investigators said Pike, then 18, saw Slemmer as a romantic rival.
Pike does not deny her part in the brutal killing. But her lawyers contend that other factors, such as her age at the time and her upbringing marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not fully understood and shared with the jury that sentenced her to death.
In her statement, Pike said, “I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.”
She said she was also grateful for the first responders, doctors and nurses who “treated me with compassion, dignity and respect.”
While she does not know what her fate may be, she said she is left “searching for meaning in what happened to me” as she has become the first person known to have survived a lethal injection after the drugs had already been administered.
“I don’t know why I survived that night,” she added. “I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone.”

NASHVILLE, United States — Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row prisoner who survived an attempt to execute her by lethal injection, says she continues to suffer physical and emotional pain a month after the failed procedure.
Pike, 50, described her condition in a statement released through her lawyers on Friday, October 30, 2026, marking her first public comments since the state unsuccessfully attempted to carry out her death sentence.
She said she had expected to die when she entered the execution chamber but regained consciousness days later in hospital, where she was receiving emergency treatment.
The prisoner reported persistent pain throughout her body, particularly in her arms, hands, and throat. She also said speaking remained difficult.
“There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said in the statement released through her attorneys.
Although she acknowledged that her physical condition was improving, she distinguished recovery from the wider consequences of the experience.
“But healing is not the same as being okay,” she said.
Execution Attempt Leaves Prisoner Hospitalised
Pike was scheduled to die on September 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old fellow student.
She was convicted of participating in Slemmer’s killing, which involved a prolonged assault in which the victim was beaten and stabbed.
The execution proceeded with the administration of two doses of pentobarbital, the drug used in Tennessee’s lethal injection procedure.
Pike did not die.
She was subsequently transferred to hospital, where she required a ventilator. Her lawyers initially expressed serious concerns about her chances of survival.
She later regained consciousness and began speaking and walking with assistance.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the first person known to have survived an execution attempt in which lethal injection chemicals were actually administered.
She spent approximately 10 days in hospital before being returned to prison, where she has continued receiving medical treatment.
In her statement, Pike said she had spent 28 years in solitary confinement and was now experiencing renewed isolation in the prison’s medical ward.
She described the separation from other prisoners and personal contacts as another source of distress.
Tennessee Investigates Failed Execution
The circumstances surrounding Pike’s survival have prompted an official investigation and renewed legal proceedings over whether Tennessee can attempt to execute her again.
Governor Bill Lee ordered an inquiry into the failed procedure and postponed another execution scheduled for later in the year.
Pike’s lawyers are pursuing legal action to prevent the state from making a second attempt.
They had challenged Tennessee’s lethal injection procedures before the execution, arguing that the state’s revised protocol presented unacceptable risks.
Following the unsuccessful procedure, the legal team sought permission to update its complaint to incorporate the events of September 30.
According to CNN’s report, a court granted Pike additional time to submit the amended filing because of her medical condition.
The legal challenge could determine whether the state may proceed with another execution.
Lee has indicated that he does not intend to commute the death sentence.
Speaking to reporters in Nashville earlier in the week, the governor said he expected Pike’s punishment to remain unchanged unless a court ruled otherwise.
Victim’s Family Expresses Frustration
The failed execution has also brought renewed anguish to Slemmer’s relatives.
Her mother, May Martinez, has criticised the state’s handling of the procedure and expressed frustration that public attention has increasingly concentrated on Pike’s medical condition rather than her daughter’s murder.
“I think the state owes me a big apology,” Martinez told CNN affiliate WTLV.
Pike acknowledged the suffering of Slemmer’s relatives in her statement, saying she continued to think about the consequences of the killing for the victim’s family.
She also expressed gratitude to the emergency responders, doctors, and nurses who treated her after the execution attempt.
Pike thanked her lawyers and supporters, including people she had never met, for their assistance and messages of encouragement.
Her statement offered no indication that she knew what would happen next.
For now, she remains in prison under a death sentence, receiving medical treatment while her lawyers pursue a challenge to any further attempt to execute her.
The state’s investigation is continuing, and no new execution date has been announced.

“Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison’s medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me,” Pike said. “That isolation brings its own kind of pain. I spent 28 years in solitary confinement and much of what I am experiencing today is a repeat of that condition.”
She also expressed gratitude for her attorneys as well as “the first responders, doctors, nurses and everyone at the hospital” for treating her with “compassion, dignity and respect.”
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” she said. “Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone.”
Pike’s attorneys have repeatedly called for Gov. Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life without the possibility of parole. In light of her botched execution, just months after the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers was called off because of problems placing IV lines, Lee announced that no more executions would take place in Tennessee this year. But earlier this week, he indicated that he is not likely to commute Pike’s death sentence before he leaves office.
“As it related to a particular individual like Christa Pike and her crime, she’s still incarcerated under the laws of the State of Tennessee,” Lee told reporters. “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
Physician explains himself
Also speaking for the first time since Pike’s failed execution was Dr. Mark Fowler, the physician contracted by the state to participate in executions. Fowler was also at the center of the botched Carruthers execution. His role in the state’s death penalty is only known publicly because Riverbend Warden Kenneth Nelsen revealed his identity within earshot of witnesses during the 2025 execution of Byron Black.
The physician, who has no hospital privileges and whose participation in executions goes against the American Medical Association’s code of ethics, has made few public statements since May. But he recently spoke at length to New York Magazine, insisting he is “not incompetent,” describing the failed Carruthers and Pike executions and explaining his reasoning for playing such a significant role in Tennessee’s death penalty.
“How can you morally say, ‘I’m for the death penalty so long as somebody else does the work?’” he told New York’s Rachel Corbett. “I do things that nobody wants to do.”
Fowler said he does not see a contradiction between his oath as a doctor, or beliefs as an evangelical Christian, and his role as an executioner and also told Corbett that he would “like to be remembered as a Renaissance man.”

sources.news_title: Bill Lee Pauses Tennessee Executions Orders Independent Review
sources.text:
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to determine what went wrong during the attempted execution of Christa Pike, the first woman scheduled to be put to death in the state in more than two centuries.
The decision follows a visibly troubled lethal injection procedure that left Pike alive and raised fresh questions about the state’s execution protocols. When pressed by reporters this week on whether a second attempt would proceed, Lee said: “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
The governor’s response has drawn criticism from advocates who argue the focus remains narrowly on procedure rather than the penalty itself. “I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out,” said Mann, speaking on the state’s handling of the case. “What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her.”
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution deviated from plan, though it has defended the method used. The agency declined to comment on Pike’s statement when contacted by the BBC.
Among those present was May Martinez, mother of one of Pike’s victims, who had long pushed for the execution to proceed. She described the scene as a “mess” and told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida that she believes the state owes her an apology. “All I wanted was justice,” Martinez said.
Pike’s legal team had spent decades appealing her conviction. In the days leading up to the scheduled execution, both the U.S. Supreme Court and Governor Lee declined to intervene.
The episode is not the first in Tennessee to raise alarm. Earlier this year, the execution of Tony Carruthers — convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994 — was postponed after staff were unable to establish intravenous access. Lee granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve.
Nationally, the pattern is broader. In 2022, more than a third of all executions in the United States were classified as botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonpartisan research organization.
As the independent review gets underway, the pause on executions places Tennessee at the center of a renewed national debate over the reliability and humanity of lethal injection — and whether procedural fixes can resolve deeper structural concerns.
